principle: Measure multi-ion-channel effects and contractile behaviour in human stem-cell-derived cardiomyocytes and feed them into a mechanistic action potential model, so that proarrhythmic risk is predicted from integrated human electrophysiology rather than from hERG block alone, which is known to misclassify safe multi-channel blockers.
trl_basis: The approach is embedded in the CiPA regulatory-science paradigm, is used in operational safety pharmacology packages and continues to be developed in the 2026 literature; demonstrated in the operational environment without displacing the required in vivo QT assessment. [E-8090][E-8031]
developers: FDA CiPA initiative; Health and Environmental Sciences Institute; Ncardia, FUJIFILM Cellular Dynamics and Axion as platform suppliers; academic cardiac electrophysiology modellers
decisive_milestone: A regulator accepts an iPSC-cardiomyocyte plus in silico package in place of a thorough QT study or an in vivo telemetry study for a specific programme; checkable by 2030 from ICH E14/S7B question-and-answer implementation and sponsor disclosure.
remaining_hard_problems: iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes remain immature relative to adult myocardium in calcium handling and t-tubule structure; the models predict cellular repolarisation, not tissue-level reentry, which is the actual arrhythmic mechanism; and inter-laboratory variability in the cell products is substantial.
commercialization_reasoning: Already in operational use and encoded in ICH implementation questions and answers; the window covers progression from supportive to substitutive evidence.
failure_scenario: The assay reduces false positives on hERG-blocking but safe compounds - which was its design purpose - while contributing nothing to the structural and inflammatory cardiotoxicity that dominates late-stage cardiac attrition for oncology agents.
modality_scope: small molecule; some relevance to kinase inhibitor oncology

tech_name: Broad in vitro secondary pharmacology panels with target-adverse-reaction association maps
principle: Screen a candidate against a wide panel of off-targets and interpret hits against an empirical map linking each off-target to adverse reactions observed for marketed drugs, so that an off-target liability is translated into a specific predicted clinical adverse event rather than a generic flag.
trl_basis: Panels are a routine third-party service and the target-ADR association resource is published in Nature Communications with a follow-up analysis of clinically discontinued compounds; proven in operations though not required by regulation. [E-8096]
developers: Eurofins Cerep; Charles River Laboratories; Novartis and Roche safety pharmacology groups who published the association resource; FDA safety pharmacology reviewers
decisive_milestone: A published prospective analysis showing that programmes using panel-plus-association-map triage have a lower rate of clinical safety-driven discontinuation than matched programmes that do not; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Panels cover a few hundred targets out of a proteome; potency at an off-target does not translate to clinical effect without free-drug exposure at the relevant tissue, which the panel does not measure; and association maps are confounded because drugs that hit a given off-target share chemotypes and indications.
commercialization_reasoning: Long-established commercial practice; the incremental technology is the association map, which is published and freely usable now.
failure_scenario: The panel identifies liabilities that medicinal chemists cannot engineer out without losing primary potency, so the information arrives without an actionable response and programmes proceed anyway.
modality_scope: small molecule primarily

tech_name: Generative de-risking: model-guided redesign to remove a specific safety liability
principle: Use a generative model conditioned jointly on primary target activity and on a predicted safety liability to propose analogues that retain the former and lose the latter, converting safety optimisation from a screening exercise into a design objective.
trl_basis: Reported as a computational case study with a claimed 700-fold hERG affinity reduction in a redesigned compound; proof of concept in silico, with no prospective wet-lab or clinical confirmation reported. [E-8032][E-8031]
developers: Academic cheminformatics groups publishing CardioGenAI and related models; Isomorphic Labs; Recursion; Insilico Medicine; large pharma computational chemistry groups
decisive_milestone: A compound designed by conditional generative de-risking enters clinical trials and its safety margin on the specific liability is confirmed in vivo, with the design provenance disclosed; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Generative models optimise against a predictor, and optimising hard against an imperfect predictor produces molecules that exploit the predictor's blind spots rather than molecules that are safer. Multi-objective optimisation across several liabilities simultaneously has no demonstrated solution.
commercialization_reasoning: The method is at case-study stage; moving from a single retrospective example to prospective clinical confirmation requires a full discovery-to-IND cycle, roughly four to six years once a programme commits.
failure_scenario: Reward hacking against the safety predictor: the generated molecules score well on the model and fail in the assay, and the approach is abandoned as untrustworthy.
modality_scope: small molecule

tech_name: Large public human toxicogenomics reference resources
principle: Build a public, standardised dataset linking many compounds to human cellular transcriptomic responses at controlled exposures, so that any group can train and, critically, externally validate a toxicity model on the same reference instead of on proprietary internal data of unknown composition.
trl_basis: A large-scale human toxicogenomics resource for DILI prediction was published in Nature Communications and is publicly available; validated as a resource in a relevant environment, not yet embedded in decision workflows. [E-8086]
developers: Academic consortia publishing in Nature Communications; NIH Tox21 and ToxCast programmes; EU-ToxRisk successors; Broad Institute Connectivity Map lineage
decisive_milestone: Two independent groups publish DILI models trained on the resource whose prospective performance on an external compound set is within a narrow band of each other; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: Transcriptomic response at 24 hours in a cell line is a distant proxy for organ injury in a patient over months; and the compounds in any such reference are biased toward those that already failed, so the negative class is poorly defined.
commercialization_reasoning: The resource is available now; models built on it and externally validated should appear within a few years, which is the actual test of value.
failure_scenario: The resource becomes a benchmark on which models compete without any of them improving prospective decisions, repeating the pattern of earlier toxicogenomics databases.
modality_scope: small molecule
notes: also serves B10

tech_name: Droplet microfluidic ultrahigh-throughput screening with cell-free expression
principle: Compartmentalise each library member in a picolitre droplet with cell-free transcription-translation and an activity-coupled fluorescent readout, then sort at kilohertz, so that ten million protein variants can be functionally assayed in an hour without cloning into or expressing in a living host.
trl_basis: Peer-reviewed JACS demonstration of ten million variants sorted in under one hour with bifunctional bead capture; validated in a relevant environment and available in specialised laboratories, not a commodity service. [E-8054]
developers: ETH Zurich and Cambridge droplet microfluidics groups; Sphere Fluidics; Atum and enzyme engineering companies; Ginkgo Bioworks
decisive_milestone: A commercial provider offers droplet screening of 10^7 variants per campaign as a catalogue service with published turnaround and price; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: The assay must be coupled to fluorescence, which excludes most therapeutically interesting phenotypes; cell-free expression fails for membrane proteins and for anything requiring mammalian post-translational modification; and hits selected in a droplet frequently do not reproduce in cells.
commercialization_reasoning: The platform works now in expert hands; commoditisation of microfluidic instrumentation has historically taken five or more years.
failure_scenario: The technology delivers enormous throughput on the small subset of problems expressible as a fluorescence readout, and the field's actual bottleneck - phenotypic and in vivo assays - is untouched.
modality_scope: enzymes, binders, protein therapeutics
notes: LOW-VALUE FLAG: B9 elasticity point is 0.9, and library screening is already among the fastest steps in the pipeline

tech_name: Self-driving laboratories with closed-loop design-build-test-learn
principle: Let a model propose the next experiment, a robot execute it, instruments capture the result and the model update, iterating without human intervention, so that the cycle time of an optimisation campaign is set by robot throughput rather than by researcher scheduling.
trl_basis: A 2026 review states most systems marketed as self-driving operate at autonomy Level 2 with only a handful at Level 3, and the flagship demonstrations are in robotically simple chemistry; component validation with narrow demonstrations. [E-8055][E-8056]
developers: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (A-Lab); University of Toronto Acceleration Consortium; Emerald Cloud Lab; Ginkgo Bioworks; Chemify; academic SDL groups
decisive_milestone: An independently reported campaign in which a self-driving system autonomously optimises a therapeutically relevant biological property - not a materials or reaction-yield property - over at least fifty closed-loop iterations without human intervention; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Biological assays fail in ways that require human diagnosis; sample handling for cells and tissues is far less robust than for liquids; and the model must know when its own uncertainty means the next experiment should be a control rather than an exploration, which no deployed system does reliably.
commercialization_reasoning: Level 3 autonomy exists in narrow chemistry now; extension to biology requires assay robustness improvements that are incremental and slow, and full autonomy in biology has no announced credible milestone.
failure_scenario: Systems reach Level 2 or 3 and stop, because every additional increment of autonomy requires handling a longer tail of failure modes; the economic case never closes against skilled technicians plus conventional automation.
modality_scope: small molecule, protein engineering, media and process optimisation
notes: LOW-VALUE FLAG: attacks a low-elasticity bottleneck and its main output is more data, whose value depends on B10 and B1

tech_name: LLM agent orchestration of laboratory workflows (Coscientist, Virtual Lab class)
principle: Use a language model as the planning layer that reads literature, writes the protocol, calls instrument APIs and interprets results, so that the expertise needed to design and execute a multi-step experiment is supplied by the model rather than by a specialist.
trl_basis: Published demonstrations include an LLM agent optimising real chemical reactions and a 2025 agent-designed nanobody set that was experimentally validated; proof of concept, with no routine third-party deployment. [E-8055]
developers: Carnegie Mellon (Coscientist); Stanford (Virtual Lab); FutureHouse; Anthropic and OpenAI research collaborations; academic agent laboratories
decisive_milestone: An agent-designed and agent-executed experimental campaign produces a molecule or biologic that enters IND-enabling studies, with the agent's role documented; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Agents cannot currently detect that an experiment failed for a mundane physical reason rather than a scientific one; hallucinated protocol steps are unsafe in a wet laboratory; and there is no accepted way to attribute or audit responsibility for an agent-designed experiment.
commercialization_reasoning: Current demonstrations are single-campaign research results; safe deployment in a regulated or even a GLP-adjacent environment requires audit and safety layers that do not exist.
failure_scenario: Agents remain useful for literature synthesis and protocol drafting and are never trusted to close the loop, so the bottleneck - physical execution and interpretation - is unchanged.
modality_scope: all modalities in discovery

tech_name: Cloud laboratories and remote-execution experimental APIs
principle: Expose a fully instrumented laboratory as a programmable service so that an experiment is submitted as code, executed by a remote facility and returned as structured data, decoupling experimental capacity from a research group's own equipment and staff.
trl_basis: Cloud laboratories operate commercially and execute third-party protocols in production; demonstrated in the operational environment, not 9 because coverage of assay types remains narrow and adoption is a small share of research spend. [E-8055]
developers: Emerald Cloud Lab; Strateos lineage; Ginkgo Bioworks Reconfigurable Automation Carts; large pharmaceutical internal automation platforms
decisive_milestone: A published drug discovery programme executes the majority of its experimental work through cloud laboratory APIs from hit identification to candidate selection; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: The assay catalogue is limited to what the facility has automated, which excludes bespoke biology; latency and shipping for cells and tissues constrain the experiment types; and troubleshooting an unexpected result remotely is slower than at the bench.
commercialization_reasoning: Commercially available now; the window reflects the period over which assay coverage broadens enough for majority-of-programme use.
failure_scenario: Cloud execution is efficient for standardised assays that were never the bottleneck, and every programme retains a local wet laboratory for the non-standard work, so total cycle time is unchanged.
modality_scope: all modalities in discovery
notes: LOW-VALUE FLAG: standardised assays are not the constraint

tech_name: Image-based optical pooled screening in primary cells and tissues (PerturbView class)
principle: Read perturbation identity in situ by sequencing a barcode directly inside fixed cells, so that a pooled genetic screen can use rich morphological imaging as its phenotype, in primary cells and tissue sections rather than only in dissociable cell lines.
trl_basis: Method published with demonstration in primary cells and tissues; validated in a relevant environment and being commercialised, but not yet a routine service. [E-8097][E-8012]
developers: Broad Institute (Blainey and Carpenter groups); Whitehead Institute; Ramanathan and colleagues (PerturbView); 10x Genomics and imaging platform vendors
decisive_milestone: A commercial provider offers image-based pooled screening in primary human cells at genome scale with published cost and turnaround; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Barcode detection efficiency in thick tissue limits the practical library size; morphological phenotypes need very large training sets to become interpretable; and imaging throughput, not library size, becomes the constraint.
commercialization_reasoning: The method is published and being commercialised; single-cell method commoditisation historically runs three to five years.
failure_scenario: Morphological readouts prove hard to map onto disease-relevant phenotypes, so screens generate rich data whose biological interpretation requires the same follow-up work the screen was meant to avoid.
modality_scope: target discovery across modalities
notes: also feeds B1

tech_name: Cross-pharma federated learning consortia (MELLODDY lineage, K-MELLODDY, Apheris)
principle: Train a shared model across partners' private datasets by exchanging model updates rather than data, so that the effective training set is the union of every partner's proprietary assay history without any partner disclosing its compounds or results.
trl_basis: MELLODDY federated 2.6 billion activity points across ten companies with published aggregated model improvements, and successor programmes are running in Korea and through commercial platforms; validated in a relevant environment, with the original consortium concluded rather than converted into standing infrastructure. [E-8057][E-8060][E-8088]
developers: MELLODDY consortium (ten pharmaceutical companies, Owkin, Iktos, academic partners); K-MELLODDY (Korea); Apheris; NVIDIA FLARE community
decisive_milestone: A standing, funded federated infrastructure operating continuously across at least five pharmaceutical companies for three consecutive years, with published model performance deltas; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Batch effects between contributing sites can impair federated model performance independently of privacy design; partners' assay protocols differ enough that the same nominal endpoint is not the same measurement; and the incentive to contribute high-quality data is weak when benefit is shared.
commercialization_reasoning: The technical demonstration is complete; what is missing is a sustainable governance and funding vehicle, which is an institutional rather than technical timeline.
failure_scenario: Performance gains are real but small - a few points of AUC - and do not justify the legal and infrastructure overhead, so consortia dissolve at the end of each grant cycle, as the original one did.
modality_scope: small molecule ADMET and QSAR primarily

tech_name: Precompetitive open data generation programmes (LIGAND-AI)
principle: Fund the deliberate generation of new experimental data - including negative results and systematically sampled chemical space - and place it in the public domain, rather than mining data generated for other purposes, so that the training distribution is designed rather than inherited.
trl_basis: LIGAND-AI launched in 2026 with reported funding around EUR 60 million and named industrial and academic partners; the programme exists and is funded but has not yet released data or demonstrated model improvement. [E-8058]
developers: Innovative Health Initiative; Pfizer; Structural Genomics Consortium; Goethe University Frankfurt; Abcam; participating pharmaceutical companies and hospitals
decisive_milestone: Public release of a protein-small-molecule interaction dataset from the programme, together with an independent demonstration that models trained with it outperform models trained without it on a held-out prospective task; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Deciding which negatives to generate is itself a modelling problem - uniformly sampled negatives are uninformative and adversarially chosen negatives encode the current model's biases; and assay standardisation across contributing sites is the same unsolved problem that limits federated learning.
commercialization_reasoning: Programme funding runs several years before substantial data release; independent validation of benefit follows release by one to two years.
failure_scenario: The programme produces a large, clean dataset in a chemical and target space that the field had already covered, because the partners contribute what is easy rather than what is missing.
modality_scope: small molecule; protein-ligand interaction
notes: one of very few technologies aimed at negative data specifically

tech_name: Standardised immutable benchmarks with enforced evaluation protocols (Polaris, Virtual Cell Challenge)
principle: Freeze datasets and evaluation splits in a hosted registry that participants cannot modify, so that reported model performance is comparable across groups and the field can tell whether a claimed improvement is real - which is the precondition for knowing whether more data helps.
trl_basis: Polaris operates as a public benchmarking platform with deliberately limited flexibility for reproducibility, and the Virtual Cell Challenge is published in Cell; operational infrastructure whose influence on the field's reporting norms is not yet established. [E-8059][E-8008]
developers: Polaris Hub (Valence Labs and partners); Arc Institute (Virtual Cell Challenge); Therapeutics Data Commons; MLCommons science working groups
decisive_milestone: A major journal or a major pharmaceutical company adopts a benchmark registry result as a required element of a method claim, replacing self-reported held-out performance; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: A frozen benchmark is gamed over time as the community overfits to it, and refreshing it destroys comparability; and benchmark tasks are chosen for tractability rather than for correspondence to a decision anyone makes.
commercialization_reasoning: Infrastructure is operational; norm adoption depends on editorial and industrial policy decisions that could happen quickly or not at all.
failure_scenario: Benchmarks are adopted enthusiastically and overfit within two years, so leaderboard position stops correlating with prospective usefulness - the pattern already seen in molecular property prediction.
modality_scope: small molecule, protein, single-cell

tech_name: Industrial perturbation data factories as a purpose-built training corpus
principle: Operate a dedicated high-throughput single-cell platform whose product is the dataset rather than a drug, running planned combinatorial perturbation designs at a scale no individual laboratory reaches, so that the training corpus is designed for model fitting instead of scavenged from publications.
trl_basis: Tahoe-100M was produced, released and heavily redistributed, and a four-fold larger successor with 225,000 perturbation interactions was announced in January 2026; this is a functioning industrial operation. [E-8006][E-8007]
developers: Tahoe Therapeutics (Mosaic platform); Arc Institute; Chan Zuckerberg Biohub; Recursion Pharmaceuticals phenomics; Insitro
decisive_milestone: A model trained on a purpose-built perturbation corpus outperforms the same architecture trained on public scavenged data on a prospective, externally held task; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: Scale in cell lines does not substitute for diversity in biology - fifty cancer lines and a few thousand chemicals span a narrow slice of human physiology; and single-cell transcriptome is one readout among many that matter.
commercialization_reasoning: The data are already commercial; the value question resolves within a few years as models trained on them are prospectively evaluated.
failure_scenario: The corpus improves models on tasks resembling the corpus and not on tasks that matter, and the field discovers it has scaled the wrong axis - more perturbations of the same fifty cell lines rather than more biological contexts.
modality_scope: oncology-weighted small molecule and biologics

tech_name: Self-driving laboratories as designed data generators, including negatives
principle: Point a closed-loop autonomous platform at the goal of maximising information rather than maximising hits, so that the experiments run are the ones the model is most uncertain about - which systematically produces the negative and boundary-condition data that human-run campaigns never publish.
trl_basis: Self-driving platforms exist at autonomy Level 2-3 but are configured for optimisation, not for information-maximising data generation; the specific application is a concept with component validation only. [E-8055][E-8056]
developers: University of Toronto Acceleration Consortium; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; Emerald Cloud Lab; academic active-learning groups; Ginkgo Bioworks
decisive_milestone: A published dataset generated by an active-learning autonomous platform, containing a designed balance of positives and negatives, is shown to improve model performance more per experiment than an equally sized conventionally generated dataset; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Active learning requires a calibrated uncertainty estimate, which current biological models do not provide; and information-maximising experiments are individually uninteresting, so no one funds them without a separate mechanism.
commercialization_reasoning: Depends on self-driving laboratories reaching reliable Level 3 in biology, which is itself a late-decade prospect, plus a funder willing to pay for data rather than for discoveries.
failure_scenario: No one pays for negative data. The platforms are owned by companies whose incentive is to find hits, and the boundary-condition data stay unmeasured and unpublished.
modality_scope: all modalities
notes: DEPENDENCY: presupposes B9 self-driving labs reach reliable autonomy - a technology whose own bottleneck is unsolved

tech_name: Government-brokered multi-state outcomes-based agreements (CMS Cell and Gene Therapy Access Model)
principle: Have a single public payer negotiate an outcomes-linked price on behalf of many state programmes at once, with rebates if the therapy underperforms, so that a payer facing a one-time seven-figure cost is insulated from durability risk and a manufacturer faces one negotiation instead of fifty.
trl_basis: Operating with 33 states plus DC and Puerto Rico covering about 84 percent of Medicaid sickle cell beneficiaries, with negotiated terms in place with both manufacturers and up to USD 9.55 million per state in implementation funding; demonstrated in the operational environment with no outcome evaluation published. [E-8061]
developers: CMS Innovation Center; state Medicaid agencies; Vertex Pharmaceuticals; Genetix Biotherapeutics (formerly bluebird bio); CIBMTR as outcomes registry
decisive_milestone: CMS publishes utilisation and outcome data showing that annual gene therapy treatment starts among Medicaid sickle cell beneficiaries in participating states are at least double the pre-model annual baseline; checkable by 2029 from CMS model evaluation reports.
remaining_hard_problems: Outcomes-based agreements require an outcome measurable within a payer's patience horizon, and durability of a one-time therapy is by definition a long-horizon question; patient mobility between payers breaks the link between who pays and who benefits; and the administrative burden of tracking outcomes has historically exceeded the rebate value.
commercialization_reasoning: The model is running with state start dates through January 2026 and a defined evaluation period, so evidence on whether it changes access arrives within a few years.
failure_scenario: Uptake stays low because the barrier was never price alone - it was the availability of transplant-capable centres, the myeloablative conditioning burden and patient willingness - so the model demonstrates that price was not the binding constraint.
modality_scope: gene therapy and cell therapy; one-time high-cost treatments
notes: the only technology here that directly attacks payment for durable one-time therapies Milestone quantified under the X-25 principle.

tech_name: Transferable priority review vouchers as a pull incentive
principle: Award a tradeable entitlement to expedited review for developing a product in a commercially unattractive area, so that the developer monetises the voucher on the open market and the reward is funded by another company's willingness to pay for speed rather than by an appropriation.
trl_basis: A decade-old operating programme reauthorised through September 2029 with an active secondary market at roughly USD 80-150 million per voucher; proven in operations, not 9 because the causal effect on programme initiation is contested. [E-8062]
developers: U.S. Congress; FDA; voucher-holding sponsors and purchasers; Duke-Margolis and academic policy evaluators
decisive_milestone: A published quasi-experimental evaluation using the 2024 lapse and 2026 reauthorisation as a natural experiment reports a change of at least 20 percent in the annual count of rare pediatric programme initiations, with a confidence interval excluding zero; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: The voucher rewards approval, not need, so it can pay for products that would have been developed anyway; its value depends on a secondary market whose price has been volatile; and it consumes review capacity, so the benefit to one sponsor is partly a cost to others.
commercialization_reasoning: Already operating; the reauthorisation to 2029 defines the current policy horizon.
failure_scenario: The programme is shown to be paying largely for products that would have been developed regardless, and Congress declines to reauthorise it again in 2029.
modality_scope: rare pediatric disease, tropical disease, medical countermeasures
notes: Milestone quantified under the X-25 principle.

tech_name: Synthetic royalty monetisation and non-dilutive structured finance
principle: Sell a defined slice of future product revenue to a specialist investor for cash today, so that a developer converts an asset's expected cash flows into development capital without issuing equity at a depressed valuation or taking on debt with covenants it cannot meet.
trl_basis: Roughly USD 2.7 billion in reported royalty transactions in the first half of 2025 alone and near-universal executive intent to consider the instrument; proven in operations, not 9 because it is available almost exclusively to companies with approved or near-approved products. [E-8063]
developers: Royalty Pharma; Blackstone Life Sciences; HealthCare Royalty; DRI Capital; sponsor chief financial officers
decisive_milestone: Disclosed royalty-monetisation transactions against assets not yet approved reach at least 20 percent of annual volume and at least USD 1 billion per year, sustained over two consecutive years; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: The instrument prices risk that the seller understands better than the buyer, so it works best precisely where uncertainty is lowest - which is not where capital is scarcest. It does nothing for preclinical and early clinical assets, where the funding gap actually sits.
commercialization_reasoning: Mature and growing market; no technical development required.
failure_scenario: Royalty capital continues to concentrate on de-risked late assets, so the early-stage funding gap that drives attrition is untouched and the instrument simply reallocates returns among late-stage investors.
modality_scope: all modalities; late-stage and marketed assets
notes: LOW-VALUE FLAG: attacks the part of the capital chain that is least constrained Milestone quantified per X-25.

tech_name: Focused Research Organizations as mission-scoped non-dilutive vehicles
principle: Fund a time-limited organisation with a single defined deliverable - a tool, dataset or process that is too applied for academia and too unprofitable for a company - at roughly USD 25-75 million over five to seven years, then wind it down and place the output in the commons.
trl_basis: A developed policy proposal with defined budgets and structures, and a small number of operating instances; the concept is validated in a relevant environment but the model has not been shown to deliver at the scale proposed. [E-8064]
developers: Federation of American Scientists; Convergent Research; Schmidt Futures and philanthropic funders; NIH and ARPA-H as potential public funders
decisive_milestone: At least five FROs complete their mandates and their outputs are demonstrably used as standard infrastructure by third parties; checkable by 2031.
remaining_hard_problems: The model assumes the deliverable can be specified in advance, which is exactly what is uncertain for the hardest infrastructure problems; and wind-down means no one maintains the output after year seven, which is when most research infrastructure needs maintenance most.
commercialization_reasoning: Existing instances are mid-mandate; a track record sufficient for the model to become a standard funding instrument needs at least one full cohort to complete, which is late in the decade.
failure_scenario: FROs deliver their artefacts and nobody maintains them; the tools decay within three years of wind-down and the field returns to the fragmented status quo.
modality_scope: modality-agnostic research infrastructure
notes: the natural vehicle for B10 data infrastructure, which no company will fund alone

tech_name: Harmonised EU joint clinical assessment as a single-evidence-package mechanism
principle: Replace parallel national clinical assessments with one EU-level joint clinical assessment, so that a developer prepares one comparative evidence package instead of twenty-seven, shortening the aggregate time and cost from approval to reimbursement decisions.
trl_basis: In force since January 2025 for oncology medicines and advanced therapies, extending to orphan products in 2028 and all products in 2030; operating in the real environment with a first-year experience record but no measured effect on access timing. [E-8065]
developers: European Commission DG SANTE; EU HTA Coordination Group; national HTA bodies; EFPIA member companies; EUnetHTA legacy consortium
decisive_milestone: A published analysis shows that time from EU marketing authorisation to first national reimbursement decision has fallen for JCA-scope products relative to the pre-2025 baseline; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: Member states retain final authority on value, pricing and reimbursement, so the joint assessment adds a step rather than replacing national ones; and requiring all relevant PICOs across member states can multiply the indirect treatment comparison workload rather than reducing it.
commercialization_reasoning: Phased implementation is fixed by regulation through 2030, so the technology's full scope and its measured effect both arrive on that schedule.
failure_scenario: The PICO multiplication effect dominates: developers must produce more comparative analyses than before, evidence generation cost rises, and national decisions are unchanged because member states give the joint assessment only nominal regard.
modality_scope: all modalities in the EU
notes: could plausibly worsen rather than relieve B11; flagged as ambiguous-sign

tech_name: Advance market commitments and pull funding for uncommercial indications
principle: Commit in advance to purchase a specified quantity of a product meeting pre-agreed criteria at a pre-agreed price, so that a developer faces a defined market for a product that would otherwise have none, without the funder needing to pick which technical approach will win.
trl_basis: The mechanism has been executed at scale in vaccines with a defined precedent and is documented as a standing policy instrument; demonstrated operationally, with limited application outside vaccines and pandemic countermeasures. [E-8099]
developers: Gavi; World Bank; BARDA; Wellcome Trust; Center for Global Development economists who designed the mechanism
decisive_milestone: An advance market commitment is executed for a non-vaccine therapeutic area - antibiotics being the canonical case - with at least one product delivered against it; checkable by 2031.
remaining_hard_problems: Setting the price and volume correctly requires knowing the cost of a product that does not exist; the commitment must be credible across political cycles longer than any government's term; and for chronic-use therapeutics the volume commitment conflicts with stewardship goals, as the antibiotic case shows.
commercialization_reasoning: Antibiotic subscription models are being legislated and piloted in several jurisdictions; a decade is a reasonable horizon for a demonstrated non-vaccine execution.
failure_scenario: The commitment is set too low to change investment decisions, because the political willingness to pay is calibrated to current prices rather than to the cost of the missing product.
modality_scope: antibiotics, vaccines, countermeasures, neglected disease

tech_name: USPTO AI-assisted invention inventorship framework (2025 revised guidance)
principle: Set an explicit administrative rule that inventorship attaches to natural persons who make a significant contribution, and abandon the joint-inventorship factor test as inapplicable to a non-human tool, so that a company using generative models to produce candidate sequences knows in advance whether and how its output can be claimed.
trl_basis: Formal published guidance in the Federal Register, in force and applied by examiners, replacing earlier guidance; proven in operations, not 9 because the rule has not been tested through appellate litigation. [E-8066]
developers: USPTO; U.S. Congress; Federal Circuit through eventual case law; patent bar and biotechnology industry groups
decisive_milestone: A Federal Circuit decision applies the 2025 framework to an AI-generated biological sequence and resolves what human contribution suffices; checkable by 2031.
remaining_hard_problems: The rule tells you inventorship attaches to humans but not how much human contribution suffices when a model generates ten thousand sequences and a human selects one; and enablement and written description for a computationally generated genus remain governed by Amgen v. Sanofi, which the guidance does not address.
commercialization_reasoning: The guidance is in force now; the remaining uncertainty is judicial rather than administrative.
failure_scenario: The framework is superseded by litigation that draws a line elsewhere, and the intervening period of uncertainty causes companies to under-file on computationally derived assets.
modality_scope: all modalities; biologics sequence claims most affected
notes: B12 elasticity point is 0.3 - among the lowest in the matrix

tech_name: Mass AI-generated defensive publication to establish prior art
principle: Generate and publish very large numbers of enabling technical disclosures across a sequence or chemical space, so that competitors cannot later patent within that space, converting freedom to operate from a licensing problem into a publication problem.
trl_basis: Described as an emerging strategy in legal commentary, with the legal standing of AI-generated disclosures explicitly ambiguous on enablement and public accessibility; concept demonstrated without validated legal effect. [E-8068]
developers: IP.com and defensive publication services; corporate IP departments; open-source biology advocates; patent offices as arbiters
decisive_milestone: A patent office or court rejects or invalidates a claim on the basis of an AI-generated mass defensive publication; checkable by 2030 from prosecution histories and decisions.
remaining_hard_problems: Prior art must enable a skilled person to practise the invention, and a machine-generated sequence with no experimental support may not enable anything; publishing at scale also destroys the publisher's own ability to patent in that space, which few companies will accept.
commercialization_reasoning: The strategy can be executed today; whether it works depends on office and court decisions, which arrive on a litigation timescale of five or more years.
failure_scenario: Offices and courts hold that bulk machine-generated disclosures lack enablement and do not count as prior art, and the companies that pursued the strategy have given away their own patent position for nothing.
modality_scope: biologics sequences, small molecule chemical space

tech_name: AI-assisted freedom-to-operate and patent landscape analysis over sequence space
principle: Search issued patents, applications, preprints and sequence databases with models that understand sequence similarity and claim scope, so that an FTO opinion for a computationally generated candidate can be produced before rather than after the molecule is advanced.
trl_basis: Commercial tools are marketed and used for layered analyses such as ADC antibody-linker-payload freedom to operate; validated in a relevant environment, with accuracy not independently benchmarked. [E-8100]
developers: Cypris; PatSnap; Clarivate and Questel; corporate IP departments; specialist biotechnology patent firms
decisive_milestone: An independent benchmark comparing AI-generated FTO opinions against attorney opinions on a blinded set of at least fifty candidate molecules, with agreement rates published; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: Claim scope is a legal construction that depends on prosecution history and doctrine of equivalents, neither of which is reliably extractable by sequence similarity; and a false negative in FTO is a catastrophic, not a recoverable, error.
commercialization_reasoning: Tools are commercially available now; the window covers the period to accepted use as a first-pass filter under attorney supervision.
failure_scenario: The tools miss a blocking claim in an unexpected family, a programme is enjoined, and the class of tools loses professional acceptance for anything beyond landscape visualisation.
modality_scope: all modalities; ADC and antibody most acute

tech_name: AI copilots embedded in electronic laboratory notebooks and scientific workflows
principle: Put a model inside the tools scientists already use so that data interrogation, protocol drafting and literature synthesis are done conversationally, raising the output of the existing workforce rather than requiring new hires.
trl_basis: Vendor survey reports 89 percent of scientists using copilots as their first step for interrogating data, and internal upskilling supplying most AI talent; deployed in the operational environment, with the productivity claim resting on vendor-collected self-report. [E-8069]
developers: Benchling; Dotmatics; Scispot and ELN vendors; large pharmaceutical internal platform teams; foundation model providers
decisive_milestone: A controlled study inside a pharmaceutical organisation reports experiments per scientist per quarter, or time from question to answer, before and after copilot deployment with the measurement method published; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: There is no measurement of scientific output that survives the objection that the copilot changed what scientists chose to do as well as how fast they did it; and copilot fluency can substitute for, rather than build, the domain judgement that makes a senior scientist valuable.
commercialization_reasoning: Already deployed at scale; the open question is measured effect, not availability.
failure_scenario: Copilots accelerate the production of plausible-looking analyses, junior scientists stop developing the judgement to check them, and organisational absorptive capacity falls rather than rises.
modality_scope: all modalities
notes: B13 elasticity point is 0.6; this technology could plausibly have a negative sign

tech_name: Public-private apprenticeship and biomanufacturing training consortia (NIIMBL, gene therapy training networks)
principle: Combine online foundational instruction with hands-on cleanroom and bioreactor training designed jointly with the employers who will hire the graduates, so that the pipeline for cell and gene therapy manufacturing roles is built deliberately rather than by poaching.
trl_basis: NIIMBL funded eight technology and workforce projects totalling USD 9.7 million including an apprenticeship hub, and a gene therapy training network has trained cohorts; operating in the real environment at a scale far below the reported vacancy gap. [E-8070][E-8071]
developers: NIIMBL and NIST; the Wistar Institute (BioPATH); University of Houston and partner institutions; EuroGCT training providers; state workforce agencies
decisive_milestone: Annual completions from these programmes reach a level comparable to the sector's annual vacancy count in cell and gene therapy manufacturing roles, published in a sector workforce report; checkable by 2031.
remaining_hard_problems: Programme throughput is in the dozens per cohort against vacancies in the thousands; the specialised skills decay without practice, so trainees must be hired immediately; and cleanroom training capacity is itself constrained by the same facility scarcity it aims to relieve.
commercialization_reasoning: Programmes are operating now, but scaling to sector-relevant volume requires facility and instructor capacity that grows slowly and is publicly funded.
failure_scenario: The programmes train excellent candidates at a rate one to two orders of magnitude below need, and the sector continues to fill senior roles by six-to-nine-month searches and internal poaching.
modality_scope: cell and gene therapy manufacturing; biologics manufacturing

tech_name: Robotic and automation substitution for scarce technician labour
principle: Automate the repetitive physical steps in laboratory and manufacturing work so that the same output requires fewer of the technician hours that are hardest to hire, converting a labour constraint into a capital constraint.
trl_basis: Robotic isolators, closed automated cell therapy cassettes and laboratory automation are commercially deployed, but no sector-level evidence exists that automation has relieved the reported staffing shortage; validated in a relevant environment. [E-8027][E-8025][E-8039]
developers: Lonza and Miltenyi (closed cell therapy systems); Cytiva and Syntegon (isolators); Hamilton, Tecan and Opentrons (laboratory automation); Ginkgo Bioworks
decisive_milestone: A cell therapy manufacturer publishes headcount per batch before and after closed-system automation showing a sustained reduction with maintained batch success rate; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: Automation replaces the routine hours and increases demand for the scarcer skill - engineers who can qualify, troubleshoot and change-control the automated system; and validated automated systems are harder to modify, which penalises the frequent process changes that early-stage products require.
commercialization_reasoning: Equipment exists now; realising a net headcount effect requires facility redesign and revalidation, which runs several years per site.
failure_scenario: Every automated line needs an automation engineer, and automation engineers are scarcer and more expensive than the technicians they replaced, so total labour cost rises.
modality_scope: cell and gene therapy manufacturing; laboratory operations

tech_name: Universal nucleic acid synthesis order screening (SecureDNA, IBBIS Common Mechanism)
principle: Screen every synthesis order against sequences of concern using a sliding window narrow enough to catch fragmented orders, and verify the customer, so that the physical chokepoint between a digital design and a biological agent is monitored without depending on each provider building its own system.
trl_basis: Operating screening systems are deployed by providers, a federal framework sets a 200-nucleotide window tightening to 50 nucleotides by October 2026, and free open-source tooling is available; demonstrated in the operational environment with coverage gaps outside participating providers. [E-8072][E-8073][E-8074]
developers: SecureDNA Foundation; International Biosecurity and Biosafety Initiative for Science; U.S. OSTP; NIST; International Gene Synthesis Consortium members
decisive_milestone: An independent audit reports the share of global commercial synthesis capacity subject to screening, and that share exceeds ninety percent; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: Screening covers only participating providers, and benchtop synthesisers plus non-participating jurisdictions fall outside; and any list-based approach is definitionally blind to agents not on the list.
commercialization_reasoning: Deployment is underway with a fixed regulatory milestone in October 2026; broad coverage is a compliance and diplomacy timeline rather than a technical one.
failure_scenario: Screening becomes near-universal among reputable providers while synthesis capacity migrates to unscreened benchtop devices and non-participating jurisdictions, so measured coverage rises and actual risk does not fall.
modality_scope: modality-agnostic; applies to synthetic nucleic acids
notes: LOW-VALUE FLAG for drug development throughput: B14 elasticity point is 0.1, the lowest in the matrix. High societal value, negligible effect on approvals per year

tech_name: AI-resilient screening against generative protein redesign (Paraphrase Project patches)
principle: Red-team screening algorithms with AI-designed variants that preserve a toxin's structure while altering its sequence, find where the screen fails, and patch the detection logic to be structure-aware rather than sequence-similarity-based.
trl_basis: Published in Science in October 2025 following a ten-month confidential cross-sector effort, with patches reported as adopted globally; demonstrated in the operational environment, with the durability of the patches against the next model generation unknown. [E-8075]
developers: Microsoft Research; SecureDNA; IBBIS; International Gene Synthesis Consortium; participating protein design tool developers
decisive_milestone: A repeat red-team exercise against a subsequent generation of protein design models reports an evasion rate below 5 percent of tested redesigned toxin variants, against the thousands that passed undetected in the 2025 exercise; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: The defence is reactive by construction: each patch addresses the evasion strategies of the models that existed when it was written, and generative design capability is improving faster than screening logic is updated. Structure-aware screening also raises false positives against benign engineered proteins.
commercialization_reasoning: Patches are deployed now; the meaningful question is the update cadence relative to model releases, which is an ongoing operational commitment rather than a product.
failure_scenario: The patch-and-evade cycle runs permanently with the defenders one model generation behind, and screening provides assurance that is increasingly nominal.
modality_scope: modality-agnostic
notes: Milestone quantified per X-25.

tech_name: Tiered structured access and frontier model biological capability evaluations
principle: Evaluate a model's uplift on biological misuse tasks before release, and gate access to the most capable systems through vetted programmes rather than open release, with a tiered protocol governing who learns what about the evaluation results.
trl_basis: Biosecurity evaluations appear in model cards and risk frameworks across frontier laboratories, and the Frontier Model Forum has published preliminary reporting tiers; validated in a relevant environment but voluntary, unstandardised and without external verification. [E-8076]
developers: Frontier Model Forum; Anthropic, Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Meta and xAI; RAND; SecureBio; national AI safety institutes
decisive_milestone: An externally verifiable, standardised biological capability evaluation is run by a third party on at least three frontier models with comparable published results; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: Evaluations measure uplift relative to a baseline of what a determined actor could achieve without the model, and that baseline is itself unmeasured and contested; and open-weight releases make access gating unenforceable once a capable model is public.
commercialization_reasoning: The evaluation practice exists and is being standardised; external verification requires institutional arrangements that are being negotiated now.
failure_scenario: Evaluations remain self-administered and self-reported, open-weight models at comparable capability are released regardless, and structured access provides governance theatre without changing the accessible capability frontier.
modality_scope: modality-agnostic; protein and nucleic acid design tools

tech_name: Minimal residual disease as a proposed intermediate endpoint (draft guidance stage)
principle: Measure residual malignant cells at a defined sensitivity threshold at a fixed timepoint after treatment, and use negativity as an intermediate endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit, so that a trial reads out in months rather than in the years that progression-free survival requires.
trl_basis: CORRECTED under red-team finding X-24, from 8 to 6. The record contains no formal decision: the April 2024 advisory committee vote was advisory and non-binding, the January 2026 FDA document is draft guidance whose comment period closed 23 March 2026, and no drug has been approved with MRD as the primary endpoint [E-8127]. Under the scale used in this catalogue that is TRL 6, accepted into a regulatory pathway. The original 8 was also internally inconsistent: stride velocity is rated 7 precisely because no qualification exists [E-8080], and the MRD record likewise contains zero qualifications and zero approvals [E-8077].
developers: FDA Oncology Center of Excellence; EVIDENCE and i2TEAMM meta-analysis consortia; Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center; Adaptive Biotechnologies and flow cytometry assay providers; International Myeloma Working Group
decisive_milestone: FDA finalises the MRD guidance and at least one myeloma drug receives accelerated approval with MRD negativity at a 10^-5 threshold as the primary endpoint, and its confirmatory trial subsequently verifies clinical benefit; checkable by 2031 from approval and confirmatory readouts.
remaining_hard_problems: Surrogacy is established at trial level for myeloma and does not automatically transfer to other haematological malignancies or to solid tumours; assay standardisation across flow cytometry and sequencing platforms at 10^-5 sensitivity is not complete; and MRD negativity depth may reflect treatment intensity rather than durable benefit.
commercialization_reasoning: Draft guidance is issued and sponsors are designing to it now; the first accelerated approvals on this endpoint should occur within a few years, with confirmatory verification later.
failure_scenario: Confirmatory trials show that MRD-negative patients on the new agent do not have better overall survival, discrediting the endpoint and triggering withdrawal of accelerated approvals granted on it.
modality_scope: haematological malignancy; small molecule, biologics, cell therapy
notes: CORRECTED per X-24: TRL lowered 8 to 6 and the entry renamed because MRD is not qualified [E-8127]. Position in the highest-expected-value table re-derived downward accordingly; B15 was also revised to elasticity 0.7 at rank 10 in the current matrix.

tech_name: Circulating tumour DNA as an intermediate endpoint in solid tumours
principle: Track tumour-derived DNA fragments in plasma as a quantitative measure of tumour burden that changes within weeks of treatment, so that an early molecular response can substitute for a radiographic or survival endpoint measured over years.
trl_basis: A collaborative project reports evidence supporting ctDNA as a candidate intermediate endpoint in non-small-cell lung cancer, with meta-analytic work ongoing; validated in a relevant environment without regulatory qualification for any solid tumour. [E-8079]
developers: Friends of Cancer Research ctMoniTR project; FDA Oncology Center of Excellence; Natera, Guardant Health and Foundation Medicine as assay providers; academic consortium partners
decisive_milestone: FDA accepts ctDNA response as the primary endpoint supporting an accelerated approval in a solid tumour; checkable by 2031.
remaining_hard_problems: Shedding varies by tumour type, site and burden, so ctDNA-undetectable does not mean tumour-free in low-shedding disease; tumour-informed and tumour-naive assays are not interchangeable; and the relationship between molecular response depth and survival differs by mechanism of action.
commercialization_reasoning: The myeloma MRD precedent took roughly a decade of meta-analytic work from concept to advisory committee; ctDNA in solid tumours is at an earlier stage of that same process.
failure_scenario: Trial-level surrogacy fails to hold across mechanisms - ctDNA clearance tracks cytotoxic effect but not immunotherapy benefit - so no general qualification is possible and the endpoint stays a per-programme negotiation.
modality_scope: solid tumour oncology; all therapeutic modalities

tech_name: Wearable-derived digital primary endpoints (stride velocity 95th centile)
principle: Continuously measure a physical performance variable in the participant's own environment with a validated sensor, and define the endpoint as a robust statistic of that continuous stream, so that the measurement is more sensitive to change and less dependent on a single supervised clinic assessment.
trl_basis: EMA qualified stride velocity 95th centile in July 2023 as a primary endpoint for Duchenne muscular dystrophy in patients aged four and over - the first such qualification - while FDA has qualified zero sensor-derived endpoints despite wearables appearing in over a thousand trials. [E-8078][E-8080]
developers: Sysnav; Institut de Myologie and Laurent Servais group; EMA qualification team; Duchenne patient organisations; FDA COA qualification programme
decisive_milestone: FDA issues a qualification decision for a wearable-derived endpoint, or a US approval is granted with a sensor-derived primary endpoint; checkable by 2029 from the FDA DDT qualification list.
remaining_hard_problems: Qualification is device-specific because precision requirements are device-specific, so the endpoint does not generalise across sensors and creates single-supplier dependency; and behavioural change from being monitored confounds real-world performance measures.
commercialization_reasoning: One endpoint is qualified in the EU now; FDA qualification is under review, and the EMA precedent plus the existing evidentiary package is the fastest available route.
failure_scenario: The endpoint remains a one-off: each new disease and each new sensor requires a full qualification package costing years and millions, so the count of qualified digital endpoints stays in single digits through the decade - which is exactly what the record to date shows.
modality_scope: neuromuscular disease initially; extensible to any disease with a motor endpoint
notes: the gap between 1,021 trials using wearables and zero FDA-qualified endpoints is the single most informative number in this bottleneck

tech_name: Cross-indication digital mobility biomarkers (real-world walking speed)
principle: Define a physiologically fundamental, disease-agnostic measure such as real-world walking speed and qualify it once across many indications, so that the per-indication qualification cost that has limited digital endpoints to single instances is amortised.
trl_basis: A 2026 systematic review assesses the evidence and regulatory status of real-world walking speed as a cross-indication outcome measure; the concept is validated in the literature without any regulatory qualification. [E-8101][E-8080]
developers: Mobilise-D consortium (IMI); academic digital mobility groups; EMA qualification advice pathway; wearable sensor manufacturers
decisive_milestone: A regulator qualifies a digital mobility measure with a context of use spanning more than one disease area; checkable by 2031 from EMA and FDA qualification records.
remaining_hard_problems: Cross-indication qualification requires demonstrating that the same measurement means the same thing clinically in different diseases, which is a stronger claim than any single-indication qualification and has no precedent; and the minimal clinically important difference differs by population.
commercialization_reasoning: Single-indication qualification took roughly a decade for stride velocity; a cross-indication claim is a strictly harder evidentiary problem, so a later window follows.
failure_scenario: Regulators decline cross-indication qualification on the reasonable ground that clinical meaning is disease-specific, and the field remains locked into per-indication qualification economics.
modality_scope: any disease with a mobility component

tech_name: Drug development tool qualification pathways as institutional infrastructure (DDT, COA, ISTAND)
principle: Provide a formal, published route by which a biomarker, outcome assessment or novel methodology can be qualified once for a stated context of use and then reused by any sponsor, converting per-programme negotiation into shared infrastructure.
trl_basis: The programmes operate, accept submissions and publish decisions, and ISTAND has accepted novel methodology submissions; demonstrated in the operational environment, with very low throughput relative to demand. [E-8003][E-8078][E-8080]
developers: FDA CDER Drug Development Tool qualification programmes; EMA qualification of novel methodologies; Critical Path Institute consortia; C-Path and Friends of Cancer Research as submission aggregators
decisive_milestone: Completed qualifications across FDA DDT programmes reach at least 10 per year for three consecutive years, against a historical rate below 5 per year; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Qualification requires a sponsor or consortium to fund evidence generation for a tool that will then be free to competitors, which is a classic public goods problem; and review capacity for qualification submissions competes with product review capacity within the same agency.
commercialization_reasoning: The pathways exist now; increasing throughput requires either dedicated review resourcing or a consortium funding model, neither of which is currently in place.
failure_scenario: Throughput stays at a handful of qualifications per year because no one will pay for a public good, and the pathway remains a theoretical route that almost nobody uses - the zero-qualified-wearable-endpoint record being the evidence.
modality_scope: all modalities
notes: the public goods problem here is a B11 problem wearing a B15 costume Milestone quantified per X-25.

tech_name: Machine-readable study definitions (CDISC USDM, Digital Data Flow, 360i)
principle: Represent the protocol as structured data - objectives, endpoints, eligibility, schedule of activities, and their links to biomedical concepts - so that the EDC build, the site training materials, the registry entry and the statistical analysis plan are generated from one source rather than re-keyed from a document.
trl_basis: USDM v4 exists, 360i Phase 2 reference implementations run through 2026, and the SOA Workbench emits machine-readable JSON, while about 90 percent of protocols remain unstructured documents; validated in a relevant environment without production adoption. [E-8081][E-8082][E-8103]
developers: CDISC; TransCelerate BioPharma; sponsor clinical data standards groups; EDC and CTMS vendors; ACDM community
decisive_milestone: A sponsor runs a pivotal trial in which the EDC build, site materials and registry entry are all generated from a single USDM source with no manual re-keying, and reports the study build time; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: The standard must be expressive enough for adaptive and platform designs while staying machine-checkable, and those goals conflict; and the value only materialises when every downstream system consumes the standard, which is a coordination problem across dozens of vendors.
commercialization_reasoning: Specifications complete in 2026, vendor implementation follows one to three years, sponsor migration another two to four; the compounding of these stages puts routine use in the early 2030s.
failure_scenario: Sponsors author the PDF first and export a structured file afterwards, so the structured artefact is a derived, unreliable copy and downstream systems continue to rebuild from the document.
modality_scope: all modalities

tech_name: LLM protocol authoring and automated schedule-of-activities generation
principle: Use a language model that can interpret clinical prose to convert an existing protocol into structured objects, and to draft new protocol sections against a template and a precedent library, so that the authoring and digitisation step stops being months of manual work.
trl_basis: Industry reporting from mid-2026 attributes newly feasible protocol digitisation to the convergence of capable language models with the USDM standard and validated environments; the capability is demonstrated but not shown in production use for a regulatory submission. [E-8103][E-8081]
developers: Protocol digitisation vendors presenting at DIA 2026; CDISC; sponsor clinical development operations groups; foundation model providers
decisive_milestone: A sponsor submits a protocol to a regulator that was authored through an LLM-plus-USDM pipeline, with the authoring provenance disclosed, and the review proceeds without protocol-clarity information requests; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: Protocol ambiguity is often deliberate - it preserves operational flexibility - so forcing full structure surfaces disagreements the team had not resolved; and a hallucinated eligibility criterion or visit window is a patient safety issue, requiring verification that consumes the time saved.
commercialization_reasoning: The capability exists now and the standard lands in 2026; production use requires validation under GxP computerised system expectations, which typically adds two to three years.
failure_scenario: Every generated protocol requires full human review at the same care level as writing it, because the failure mode is a subtly wrong inclusion criterion, so no time is saved.
modality_scope: all modalities

tech_name: AI-generated digital twins for prognostic covariate adjustment (PROCOVA)
principle: Forecast each participant's control-arm trajectory from their baseline data using a model trained on historical control data, and enter that forecast as a prespecified covariate, so that outcome variance attributable to baseline prognosis is removed and the same power is achieved with fewer participants.
trl_basis: Received a positive EMA qualification opinion in September 2022 as an acceptable statistical approach for primary analysis of Phase 2 and 3 trials with continuous endpoints; demonstrated in the operational regulatory environment, with the size of the real-world benefit contested. [E-8040][E-8104]
developers: Unlearn.AI; EMA Scientific Advice Working Party; Alzheimer's disease consortium data holders; academic biostatisticians developing PROCOVA-MMRM
decisive_milestone: A pivotal trial that prespecified PROCOVA reports its actual achieved variance reduction against the prespecified assumption, in a peer-reviewed publication; checkable by 2029.
remaining_hard_problems: The benefit is bounded by how much outcome variance baseline covariates can explain, which in many diseases is modest, so the 10-30 percent range may not transfer; the method needs a large, relevant historical control dataset which does not exist for novel indications; and it applies to continuous endpoints, excluding time-to-event and binary outcomes that dominate oncology.
commercialization_reasoning: Qualified since 2022 and available now; the window covers accumulation of enough prespecified uses to establish the realised effect size.
failure_scenario: Realised variance reduction in prospective trials falls well short of the retrospective simulations, and sponsors conclude the regulatory novelty risk is not worth a single-digit percentage saving.
modality_scope: continuous-endpoint indications: neurology, cardiology, metabolic
notes: also relieves B4; excluded from oncology by endpoint type

tech_name: eSource and direct EHR-to-EDC data capture
principle: Pull data that already exist in the electronic health record directly into the trial database with provenance preserved, so that the transcription step - and the source data verification built to catch transcription errors - is eliminated rather than monitored.
trl_basis: Standards and vendor implementations exist and ICH E6(R3) explicitly accommodates data-driven oversight, but adoption is limited and no large-scale demonstration of monitoring cost reduction is published; validated in a relevant environment. [E-8048][E-8081]
developers: CDISC; HL7 FHIR community; Vulcan accelerator; EDC vendors; academic medical centre informatics groups; ICH E6(R3) drafters
decisive_milestone: A multi-site pivotal trial reports the share of case report form fields populated directly from EHR without manual entry, exceeding half, together with the monitoring cost per site; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: EHR data are recorded for care and lack the precision, timing and units that protocols specify, so most fields need transformation whose correctness must itself be verified; and site-by-site EHR configuration heterogeneity means integration is a per-site project, not a per-protocol one.
commercialization_reasoning: Standards are mature and E6(R3) is final, but per-site integration cost means adoption scales slowly with the number of integrated sites rather than with sponsor intent.
failure_scenario: Per-site integration cost exceeds the monitoring savings for all but the largest and longest trials, so eSource stays confined to a few mega-trials at integrated health systems.
modality_scope: all modalities

tech_name: Risk-based quality management under ICH E6(R3)
principle: Replace uniform 100 percent source data verification and fixed monitoring visits with a prospective identification of the few data and processes that actually matter to participant safety and result reliability, and concentrate oversight there, so that operational effort scales with risk rather than with data volume.
trl_basis: ICH E6(R3) core principles and Annex 1 reached final status in September 2025 and were adopted by FDA, making risk-based quality management the governing expectation; operating in the real environment, with Annex 2 still in draft. [E-8048]
developers: ICH E6 expert working group; FDA and EMA GCP inspectorates; TransCelerate risk-based monitoring initiative; sponsor quality organisations; clinical research organisations
decisive_milestone: Inspection findings data or an industry survey shows a sustained fall in monitoring visits and source data verification percentage across sponsors, without a rise in critical inspection findings; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: Risk-based approaches require the sponsor to correctly identify critical-to-quality factors in advance, and getting that wrong is only discovered at inspection; and the conservative default of full verification persists because no organisation is rewarded for the deviations it did not find.
commercialization_reasoning: The guideline is final and adopted now; behavioural change in sponsor and CRO quality organisations historically lags guideline adoption by three to five years.
failure_scenario: Sponsors adopt the language of risk-based quality management while retaining full source data verification as an internal standard, so cost is unchanged and a new documentation layer is added.
modality_scope: all modalities

tech_name: Regulatory dose-optimisation mandate (Project Optimus and the August 2024 final guidance)
principle: Change the rule that determines what dose reaches registration: require that at least two dose levels be carried into a randomised comparison so the marketed regimen is chosen on a benefit-risk comparison in patients, instead of being inherited from the highest dose that a small escalation cohort tolerated. The instrument is regulatory rather than laboratory, and it deliberately buys calendar time to buy a better-chosen dose.
trl_basis: A formal decision in force: FDA finalised the oncology dose-optimisation guidance on 8 August 2024 [E-8107], it directs sponsors to compare two doses, preferably randomised [E-8108], and published protocol analysis shows design behaviour has already shifted, with Bayesian adoption rising from 48 percent in 2021 to 75 percent in 2024 [E-8109]. Not 9 because no approval yet rests on a randomised dose comparison as the basis for the labelled dose.
developers: FDA Oncology Center of Excellence (Project Optimus); Friends of Cancer Research; ASCO; industry biostatistics and clinical pharmacology groups; EMA and PMDA through parallel initiatives
decisive_milestone: The share of new oncology NDA and BLA approvals whose development package contains a randomised comparison of at least two doses exceeds 50 percent, and the share of oncology new molecular entities carrying a dose-related postmarketing requirement falls below 20 percent against the 33.3 percent observed for 2010-2015 approvals; checkable by 2030 from FDA approval packages [E-8111].
remaining_hard_problems: A randomised dose comparison is powered to detect a difference in response rate, not in overall survival, so two doses can look equivalent on the readout that is affordable and differ on the readout that matters. Late-onset and cumulative toxicity accrue outside the observation window used to pick the dose. Dose-optimisation cohorts add patients and months in exactly the phase where sponsors are most capital-constrained, so the requirement collides with B11.
commercialization_reasoning: The guidance is final and in force now, and protocol behaviour has already changed [E-8109]. The window closes when the first cohort of programmes designed entirely under the final guidance reaches approval, which on standard oncology timelines is the late 2020s.
failure_scenario: Sponsors satisfy the letter and not the intent: two doses are carried forward separated by a factor too small to be informative, or the low-dose arm is under-enrolled and dropped at interim, and post-approval dose reductions continue at the pre-guidance rate [E-8110].
modality_scope: oncology small molecule, ADC, bispecific and cell therapy; principle extends to other therapeutic areas
notes: B17 anchor technology. Explicitly a longer-not-shorter design change; the T cost is the price of the P gain

tech_name: Model-informed drug development: exposure-response-driven dose and regimen selection
principle: Build a quantitative pharmacokinetic and exposure-response model from all available preclinical and clinical data, and select the dose and schedule from the modelled exposure that maximises benefit-risk, rather than from the empirical dose levels that happened to be tested. This lets a dose be chosen at an exposure that was never dosed directly, and lets special populations be dosed without a dedicated trial per population.
trl_basis: A formal decision in force: FDA announced availability of ICH M15 general principles for model-informed drug development in June 2026 and continued the MIDD paired meeting programme under PDUFA VII with a standing Quantitative Medicine Center of Excellence [E-8112]. Not 9 because reliance remains programme-by-programme rather than the default basis for a labelled dose.
developers: FDA CDER and CBER Division of Pharmacometrics and the Quantitative Medicine Center of Excellence; ICH M15 expert working group; EMA modelling and simulation working party; Certara and industry clinical pharmacology groups
decisive_milestone: At least 25 completed MIDD paired-meeting programmes report a dose or schedule changed as a direct result of the modelling, and more than half of new oncology approvals in a single calendar year have a labelled dose justified by exposure-response rather than by maximum tolerated dose; checkable by 2029 from FDA programme reports and approval packages [E-8112][E-8113].
remaining_hard_problems: Exposure-response models are fitted to the doses actually studied, so extrapolating to an untested exposure relies on a functional form the data cannot distinguish. Plasma exposure is a poor surrogate for tissue exposure at the target site for many modalities. Where efficacy and toxicity share an exposure driver the model cannot separate them without a randomised contrast, which returns the problem to T-082.
commercialization_reasoning: The paired meeting programme has been operating since the 2018 pilot and ICH M15 landed in June 2026; the window closes when exposure-response justification becomes the routine basis for a labelled dose rather than a supporting argument.
failure_scenario: The model is fitted post hoc to justify a dose already chosen on other grounds, so it adds regulatory documentation and changes no decision - a failure mode that is invisible from outside because the model and the dose always agree.
modality_scope: all modalities; strongest for small molecule, biologics and ADC

tech_name: Quantitative systems pharmacology for regimen design and first-in-human dose setting
principle: Represent the target pathway mechanistically - receptor occupancy, feedback loops, cell populations - so that the model predicts what a dose and schedule will do to the biology rather than fitting an empirical exposure-response curve. This allows a schedule question that cannot be answered empirically, such as intermittent versus continuous dosing to avoid pathway adaptation, to be posed before the trial exists.
trl_basis: Accepted into a regulatory pathway and no further: FDA issued draft guidance on QSP-based dose selection for minimum anticipated biological effect level on 24 June 2026 [E-8114], submissions containing QSP have risen over a decade and are used mainly for dose and regimen selection [E-8115], but the guidance is draft and no credibility standard is settled.
developers: FDA CDER pharmacometrics reviewers; Certara QSP; Applied BioMath; Rosa & Co; academic systems pharmacology groups; large pharma quantitative pharmacology functions
decisive_milestone: FDA finalises the QSP MABEL guidance and at least 5 first-in-human starting doses per year are set on a QSP basis with the model and its acceptance criteria described in the public review documents; checkable by 2030.
remaining_hard_problems: A mechanistic model has more parameters than the available data can identify, so calibration is underdetermined and different parameterisations that fit equally well predict different optimal schedules. There is no agreed prespecified quantitative acceptance criterion for QSP credibility, and biomarker data of the quality needed to constrain the model are usually absent at the point the dose must be chosen.
commercialization_reasoning: The draft guidance is out now; finalisation typically runs one to three years, and routine reliance on mechanistic rather than empirical models needs a credibility standard that the field has not yet agreed.
failure_scenario: Reviewers treat QSP output as a narrative rather than as evidence, because two credible groups modelling the same target produce different optimal schedules and there is no adjudication rule; the models stay in the appendix.
modality_scope: biologics, bispecifics, cell engagers and immuno-oncology combinations where schedule drives outcome

tech_name: Seamless randomised dose-optimisation designs with backfill (BF-BOIN, U-BOIN, seamless Phase I/II)
principle: Replace sequential escalate-then-expand with a single design that randomises patients across candidate doses while escalation continues, monitors efficacy and toxicity jointly against a utility function, and carries two doses into a randomised comparison - so the dose decision is made from randomised within-trial evidence rather than from a cross-cohort comparison of non-randomised groups.
